# **Gemini Star Platinum**

Gemini Star Platinum is a one-of-a-kind 3D visualization of the Gemini North Telescope. Made in Unreal Engine, it offers an operator-like experience in its manual mode, while also being able to replicate 1:1 the motions of the real life telescope in its live mode. All of this packaged with an easy-to-use UI and a gorgeously rendered rendition of Mauna Kea’s summit and its many telescopes, including Gemini North.

## Features

- Beautifully modeled, physically accurate models of Gemini North (telescope and dome)  
- Motion based on mass and physical parameters derived from observatory documentation and staff expertise  
- **Manual Mode**  
  - User-controlled motions via configurable velocity and target rotation  
  - Physically constrained azimuth, elevation, cassegrain, and dome  
  - Simulated unwrap limits for azimuthal and dome rotation  
  - Simulation speed setting  
  - Pointing and tracking model for 10,000 stars, with manual offset up to 5 degrees of range  
- **Live Mode**  
  - Real-time telemetry from Gemini North TCS/ECS  
  - Telescope motions based on live data from summit  
  - Data quality validation and indicators at every step  
- Time and day selection  
- Night sky toggles for constellation outlines, celestial coordinate grid  
- 6 different camera views of the observatory, including a free camera mode

## Installation

Currently, Gemini Star Platinum can only be used in the Unreal Engine editor; there are no current plans to push for an executable build. To install, simply copy the repo to your disk and open it in Unreal Engine (project version is 5.6). To edit the code, make sure to have the appropriate plugins for Unreal integration installed on the IDE of your choice (project default is Visual Studio, not VS Code\!). You may also have issues with installing the proper C++ toolchains, as well as issues with the PATH variable on Windows. Ensure you have proper permissions on your system prior to attempting to install this project, or have Unreal setup on your system fully.

## Usage

Once loaded into Unreal Engine, using the majority of Gemini Star Platinum’s features is as simple as pressing the play button. Most of the controls can be found on the user interface itself, providing you access to motion controls, shutter and vent closing/opening, datetime selection, day cycle toggling, simulation speed, night sky texture loading, and pointing and tracking with a manual offset of up to 600 arcminutes.  

There are also separate keyboard shortcuts for modifying the camera view, including the following: (1-5) for switching between several distinct fixed camera views; (0) for switching to the free camera view; (C) for cycling between the different camera views; and (T) for togging the telescope’s 3D axial and debug lines and figures.  

Navigating the 3D space in the free camera view uses Unreal’s standard flying controls for its default pawn class. In short, to move around, hold down right click to begin moving and look around the scene. While holding down the right click, use WASD to move forward, left, back, and right respectively.

## Manual Mode

### Motion Controls

The visualized telescope has four primary motions: azimuth (left-right), elevation/altitude (up-down), cassegrain rotation, and dome rotation. The shutter and dome vents are also controllable, although only as a toggle. The red text shows the current position of the given component, while the text boxes in black and sliders display the current target position for the component. Users can also control the velocity of each component in the 2nd box/slider from the top in each section.  

Caveats: Sliders and text boxes are restrained to their own respective ranges. Azimuth has a wrap range of \[-180,+360\] degrees, elevation has a range of \[-90,0\] degrees (with \-90 corresponding to pointing at horizon, 0 corresponding to zenith), cassegrain has a range of \[-180,180\] degrees, and the dome has a wrap range of \[-270, \+270\] degrees.

### Datetime Selection

The UI includes a form for entering in a date or time. These values are assumed to be integers, with ranges typical of each value (i.e. day is limited to \[1, 31\], month \[1,12\], etc.). Year is limited to a range of \[1, 9999\]. The entire form must be completed; default values are not inputted into blank boxes. Once the form is completed, clicking the “Load Datetime” button will immediately change the time of day to what was inputted by the user. Users can also check the “Day Cycle On?” checkbox, which enables the passage of time, before pressing the “Load Datetime” for their preferred setting.  
Note: Time progresses at a rate of 1 in-game hour/1 real-life minute.

### Simulation Speed

Users can click the simulation speed button (currently “1x” in the picture) to cycle through various simulation speed settings. The options are 1x, 2x, 3x, 5x, and 10x. This button affects the motion of the sky and passage of time most significantly. For faster motion during manual control, it’s recommended to modify component velocities instead.

### Night Sky

The night sky is rendered using the Celestial Vault plug-in. The night sky texture allows for customization of the look of the sky, with two primary settings available in the app being constellation outlines and celestial grid.

### Pointing/Tracking

![][image1]  
As part of offering a comprehensive operator experience, Gemini Star Platinum implements a basic model for pointing and tracking to stars. This feature is enabled via the use of the Celestial Vault plugin, which stores a catalogue of 10,000 stars that have physical instances in world space. 		To use the feature, simply input the name of whichever specific star you want the telescope to slew to and press either the “Point” button for a one-time rotation to the star OR the “Track” button to order the telescope to continuously slew to the star, from when it first crosses above the horizon to when it crosses below it. A manual offset feature is also available, allowing users to adjust the pointing of the telescope as actual operators have to every night prior to individual observations. This offset is applied according to the telescope’s reference frame rather than celestial coordinates.

## Live Mode

Connecting the visualization to the telescope has two main prerequisites: the feed bridge located in tools/feed-bridge/[server.py](http://server.py) MUST be running, and the host computer must have the permissions and ability to access the Gemini North TCS. Once those are fulfilled, enabling the connection is as simple as clicking the “Live” button. Once you do, the icon to the right of the button will begin to indicate the status of the connection. It has 5 main states: “Disconnected”, indicating no live feed activity; “Connecting”, indicating that the program has begun trying to connect to the python bridge and TCS; “Reconnecting”, indicating that there have been failed attempts to connect to either the python bridge or TCS; “Failed”, indicating that the max number of connection attempts has been reached and no more will be made; and “Live”, indicating that the program has successfully received packets from the feed bridge.   

To run the bridge, simply run `python server.py --source (insert source)`, with the source either being `mock` or `epics`. The `epics` option only works with a valid EPICS source, which can either be the TestIOC in the same root directory as `/tools/` or the actual Gemini TCS.

How the bridge finds that EPICS source depends on where it is. A TestIOC on your own machine is found by default (UDP broadcast search, no flags needed). Reaching the real Gemini TCS goes through the workstation tunnel, which needs CA name resolution over TCP instead — pass `--name_servers`:

```
python server.py --source epics --name_servers "10.26.70.200:5064 10.26.70.200:5065"
```

For an IOC on another machine on the local network, `--ca_addr "<ip>"` points the broadcast search at that host. The two flags select mutually exclusive search modes, so passing both is an error. On startup the `epics` source reports each PV as `[ OK ]` with its current value or `[FAIL]`, which is the quickest way to tell a bad tunnel from a bad PV name. `tools/test_listen.py` runs the same check standalone, without starting the bridge.

Hovering over the status icon lets you look at the health of the connection, including whether the data is stale and how old the oldest bit of live data is. Note: These figures only update when the data is measured to be stale, otherwise data age is not reported.  
Live mode disables three sections in the UI. One, the input boxes and sliders for component target positions are disabled and set to display the target values from the internal data models. Two, the input boxes and sliders for component velocities are disabled, with their values being set to defaults reflective of real-life. Three, tracking and pointing are disabled for the duration of live mode. Currently, day and time are not retrieved from the TCS; only the motions of the telescopes are replicated in the visualization.
